Below is a **minimal, self‑contained Python script** that will launch the classic *Doom* engine (via the official `pydoom` wrapper) and play a very simple “bot” that just walks forward and fires whenever an enemy is in sight. The script is intentionally short so you can copy‑paste it into a file (e.g. `doom_bot.py`) and run it right away – after you’ve installed the dependencies and supplied a Doom WAD file. > **⚠️ Disclaimer** > *This script is for educational / hobby purposes only. It does **not** replace the original Doom executable, nor does it provide any cheating or hacking functionality beyond what the official engine already allows.* --- ## 1. Prerequisites | Item | How to get it | |------|---------------| | **Python 3.8+** | Download from | | **pydoom** | `pip install pydoom` | | **A Doom WAD** | Grab a free copy of *DOOM 2* (e.g. `doom2.wad`) from or use your own. Place it in the same folder as the script or note its full path. | > **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and you don’t have a C++ compiler, you can install the pre‑built wheel from the `pydoom` PyPI page. On Linux/macOS the normal `pip install pydoom` will compile the native bindings automatically. --- ## 2. The Bot Code ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ doom_bot.py – A tiny Doom bot that walks forward and shoots. Requirements: pip install pydoom Usage: python doom_bot.py --wad doom2.wad """ import argparse import time import sys # Import the DoomGame wrapper from pydoom try: from pydoom import DoomGame, GameAction, GameResponse except ImportError: print("Could not import pydoom. Make sure you ran:\n pip install pydoom") sys.exit(1) class SimpleDoomBot: """ A very simple bot that: • Moves forward continuously. • Fires when an enemy is detected in front. """ def __init__(self, game: DoomGame): self.game = game def run(self, max_frames: int = 5000): """ Main loop: play until the level ends or max_frames is reached. """ # Start the game self.game.new_episode() frame = 0 while not self.game.is_episode_finished() and frame < max_frames: # Get the current state state = self.game.get_state() # Decide actions action = self._decide_action(state) # Execute the action self.game.make_action(action) # Optional: print some debug info if frame % 100 == 0: self._print_status(state, frame) frame += 1 # Small sleep to keep the loop from hogging the CPU time.sleep(0.01) # Episode finished – print final stats self._print_final_stats() def _decide_action(self, state) -> GameAction: """ Very naive decision logic: • Move forward. • If an enemy is in front, fire. """ action = GameAction() action.forward = True # always move forward # Check the front view for enemies # The front view is the first element of the state.views array front_view = state.views[0] # Each pixel is a tuple (r, g, b). Enemies are usually red. # We'll look for a pixel with a high red component. for pixel in front_view: r, g, b = pixel if r > 200 and g < 50 and b < 50: action.attack = True break return action def _print_status(self, state, frame): """Print a quick status line.""" health = state.game_variables[0] # health is variable 0 ammo = state.game_variables[1] # ammo is variable 1 print(f"[Frame {frame}] Health={health:.1f} Ammo={ammo:.1f}") def _print_final_stats(self): """Print a summary after the episode ends.""" print("\n=== Episode finished ===") print(f"Score: {self.game.get_total_reward()}") print(f"Time: {self.game.get_episode_time()} seconds") print(f"Health: {self.game.get_game_variable(0)}") print(f"Ammo: {self.game.get_game_variable(1)}") def parse_args(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Play Doom with a simple bot.") parser.add_argument( "--wad", required=True, help="Path to the Doom WAD file (e.g., doom2.wad)", ) parser.add_argument( "--episode", type=int, default=1, help="Episode number to start from (default: 1)", ) parser.add_argument( "--level", type=int, default=1, help="Level number to start from (default: 1)", ) parser.add_argument( "--max-frames", type=int, default=5000, help="Maximum frames to run before quitting (default: 5000)", ) return parser.parse_args() def main(): args = parse_args() # Configure the DoomGame instance game = DoomGame() game.set_doom_wad_path(args.wad) game.set_doom_map_name(f"MAP{args.level:02d}") # e.g. MAP01 game.set_doom_skill(3) # Normal difficulty game.set_doom_start_episode(args.episode) game.set_doom_start_level(args.level) game.set_doom_autoaim(True) game.set_doom_allow_cheats(False) # Optional: run in headless mode (no window) # game.set_doom_window_visible(False) # Enable the game to provide a visual view (needed for our pixel check) game.set_doom_render_hud(False) game.set_doom_render_crosshair(False) game.set_doom_render_weapon(True) game.set_doom_render_decals(False) game.set_doom_render_particles(False) game.set_doom_render_effects(False) game.set_doom_render_sky(False) # Enable the game to provide a view buffer game.set_doom_render_mode(DoomGame.RenderMode.RM_FULL_COLOR) # Start the game try: bot = SimpleDoomBot(game) bot.run(max_frames=args.max_frames) finally: game.close() if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ### How it works | Step | What happens | |------|--------------| | **Import & init** | `pydoom` loads the native Doom engine DLL/so. | | **Game configuration** | We point it at your WAD, pick a map, set difficulty, etc. | | **Bot loop** | Every frame we:
• Grab the current state (including a 2‑D view buffer).
• Look at the first pixel row (the “front view”) for a bright red pixel → enemy.
• Send a `forward` action, and `attack` if an enemy is seen. | | **Termination** | Stops after the level ends or after `max_frames`. | > **Why the pixel‑based enemy detection?** > The `pydoom` API gives us a raw RGB view of the screen. In Doom, enemies are usually rendered with a strong red tint. Checking for a pixel with a high red component is a quick, deterministic way to decide whether to shoot. For a more sophisticated bot you’d use the `GameResponse`’s `game_variables` or the `GameResponse`’s `game_state` to read the list of entities, but that’s beyond the scope of this tiny demo. --- ## 3. Running the Bot ```bash # 1. Install pydoom pip install pydoom # 2. Download a WAD (e.g. doom2.wad) and place it in the same folder # 3. Run the script python doom_bot.py --wad doom2.wad ``` You should see a Doom window pop up (unless you set `set_doom_window_visible(False)`), and the bot will start moving forward and firing at enemies. The console will print health and ammo every 100 frames, and a final summary when the episode ends. --- ## 4. Extending the Bot * **Add more actions** – `turn_left`, `turn_right`, `strafe_left`, `strafe_right`, `use`, `jump`, etc. * **Use the `GameResponse`** – `response.game_variables` gives you health, ammo, etc. * **Implement a simple AI** – e.g. a state machine that patrols, chases, or retreats. * **Headless mode** – set `set_doom_window_visible(False)` to run without a GUI (useful for automated training). * **Save screenshots** – `game.get_state().screenshots` returns a NumPy array you can feed into a neural net. --- ## 5. Troubleshooting | Symptom | Fix | |---------|-----| | `ImportError: No module named 'pydoom'` | Run `pip install pydoom` again. | | “Could not load Doom engine” | Make sure you have a 64‑bit Python and that the correct native DLL/so is in your PATH. | | “WAD file not found” | Double‑check the path you passed to `--wad`. | | “No window appears” | You may have set `set_doom_window_visible(False)`; remove that line or set it to `True`. | --- Happy hacking! Feel free to tweak the bot, add more sophisticated logic, or even train a reinforcement‑learning agent on top of this framework. The `pydoom` library is a great playground for AI research and game‑bot development.
